content.text:
**Yes—and after researching more broadly, I would loosen the earlier recommendation. PreDist is viable, but it isn’t the obvious winner for a deadline of tomorrow at noon.** Robotics deserves serious consideration, and there are good alternatives in wearables and household energy.

The deciding factor should be: **can you turn real signals into a useful, verifiable answer—and show that training improved it?**

| Direction | Concrete project | Available data | My assessment for your deadline |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Robot monitoring** | Explain why a robot’s pick-and-place cycle looks abnormal | **voraus-AD:** 2,122 cycles, including 755 anomalous cycles across 12 anomaly types; joint motion, torque, and electrical signals. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2311.04765v1) | **Strongest robotics candidate.** Short episodes and an intuitive demo. |
| **Industrial equipment** | Tell a maintenance technician which hydraulic component is degraded | **UCI Hydraulic Systems:** 2,205 one-minute cycles; pressure, flow, temperature measurements; labelled cooler, valve, pump, and accumulator conditions. Download is 73 MB. [Dataset](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/447) | **My strongest alternative to robotics.** Small download and explicit, useful targets. |
| **Wearables / wellbeing** | Describe physiological changes associated with a stressful period | **WESAD:** 15 participants, wrist and chest measurements, neutral/stress/amusement labels, and questionnaires. [Dataset](https://ubi29.informatik.uni-siegen.de/usi/data_wesad.html) | Relatable story and clear subject holdouts. Small lab study; findings should stay within that setting. |
| **Household energy** | Answer “What drove this household’s electricity peak?” | **REFIT:** aggregate and appliance-level power for 20 homes, sampled every eight seconds. [Dataset](https://pureportal.strath.ac.uk/en/datasets/31da3ece-f902-4e95-a093-e0a9536983c4) | **Strong consumer-facing story.** Appliance measurements provide a way to check explanations. |
| **Spacecraft operations** | Highlight unusual telemetry and explain its timing and shape | **NASA SMAP/MSL:** 82 telemetry channels and 105 labelled anomaly intervals, with command information. [Original repository](https://github.com/khundman/telemanom) | Compelling theme, but anonymized channels limit meaningful diagnosis. Released values also use test-set scaling—a limitation to disclose. |
| **Sleep analysis** | Explain sleep-stage transitions and summarize a night | **Sleep-EDF:** 197 recordings with expert sleep-stage annotations; OpenTSLM already provides sleep examples and checkpoints. [Dataset](https://physionet.org/content/sleep-edfx/1.0.0/), [OpenTSLM](https://github.com/OpenTSLM/OpenTSLM) | Existing tooling may reduce setup work. Needs a distinct contribution and careful checking for pretrained-data overlap. |

**For your friends’ robotics idea, I would investigate voraus-AD first.**

A useful pitch is:

> “A robot-cell assistant that reads motion and torque signals, flags abnormal cycles, and shows the operator the evidence.”

The official repository offers a **100 Hz version around 1.1 GB**, a loader, and a baseline implementation. The dataset includes physically introduced collisions, gripping problems, and increased friction. Its data license is **CC BY-NC-SA 4.0**, which matters if you later commercialize the project. [Official repository](https://github.com/vorausrobotik/voraus-ad-dataset)

Two evaluation details matter immediately:

- The original training split contains only normal cycles. Supervised fault-description training would require a separately documented split and a baseline evaluated under that same protocol.
- Fault labels and auxiliary annotations must stay out of model inputs. The paper explicitly distinguishes them from usable signals. [Dataset protocol](https://arxiv.org/html/2311.04765v1)

**AURSAD is the narrower robotics alternative:** detecting missing or damaged screws during automated assembly. Its latest listed release has 2,045 tightening samples, but only three damaged-thread examples, and either download format is about 6.4 GB. I would prefer it if your team particularly likes the assembly-quality story. [AURSAD](https://zenodo.org/records/4559556)

**One especially relevant discovery is FactoryBench.** It already pairs industrial robot telemetry with language questions, including anomaly identification and troubleshooting. That could save annotation work. However, its dataset card and paper disagree about licensing and public splits, and the hosted viewer currently shows a schema error. I would inspect a small subset before making it your dependency. [Dataset and documentation](https://huggingface.co/datasets/FactoryBench/FactoryBench), [Paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.07675v1)

For the nonrobotics options, the product differences are worth considering:

- **Hydraulics:** “Which component needs attention?” Clear labels make assessment straightforward. Explanations would need to be built from measured signal behaviour; the labels alone don’t prove a detailed causal story.
- **REFIT:** “Which appliances contributed most to this peak, and when?” Start with measured appliance channels as inputs. Inferring appliances from the whole-home meter is an additional, harder task.
- **WESAD:** “What changed in these wearable signals during this interval?” Hold out entire people and describe the experimental conditions accurately.

**My shortlist for your team would be voraus-AD, hydraulic condition monitoring, and REFIT.** My judgment is that robotics gives you the strongest live-demo story, hydraulics offers the simplest initial data preparation, and REFIT offers the most immediately understandable consumer benefit.

Before committing, I’d spend **45–60 minutes inspecting examples from the top two**: load normal and abnormal cases, plot a handful of channels, and draft five answers whose claims you can actually verify. Your $1,000 credits are useful; the immediate bottleneck is choosing a task with trustworthy targets and a training pipeline you can finish.
So, how should we continue, can you please give me a short summary of what the findings are.

We found three strong directions for tomorrow’s noon deadline:

| Option | What you demonstrate | Main advantage |
|---|---|---|
| **Robotics — voraus-AD** | Detect abnormal robot movements and explain the supporting sensor signals | Strong demo story; about 2,100 labelled cycles |
| **Hydraulic equipment — UCI** | Identify degraded pumps, valves, or cooling components | Small dataset with clear component-condition labels |
| **Home energy — REFIT** | Explain which appliances caused an electricity peak | Relatable problem with measurable explanations |

**My recommendation is to explore robotics first**, given your team’s interest. Use voraus-AD and frame it as **detecting and explaining abnormal execution**, rather than predicting future breakdowns. PreDist remains viable, but its sparse faults make it less attractive under your deadline.

The next step is a **one-hour feasibility check**: inspect several normal and faulty robot cycles, identify useful sensor channels, and confirm that a small OpenTSLM model runs on Nebius. If that works, commit to one TimeNet connector, one fine-tuned model, one baseline, and a replay demo. If it doesn’t, hydraulic condition monitoring is the fallback.

The main uncertainty is whether the data supports useful explanations—not whether you have enough compute credits.

| Source | What it provides | How it fits |

| **FactoryNet** | Industrial sensor sequences, normal/faulty executions, and standardized command/current/motion channels | Useful training data, but language targets still need checking or construction. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.09081v2) |
| **FactoryBench** | Robot telemetry paired with questions and answers about operating state, anomalies, and troubleshooting | Closest match to the challenge’s **signals → language** requirement. [Dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/FactoryBench/FactoryBench) |
| **FAA SDRS** | Aircraft malfunction and maintenance reports | Useful text, but I found no corresponding sensor recordings in this source. We cannot treat unrelated robot or aircraft signals as matching those reports. [FAA description](https://www.faa.gov/av-info/download_SDR) |

Small correction: the linked **FactoryBench paper is from 2026**, rather than 2024.

I suggest this project definition:

> **A robot-cell assistant that examines a recorded execution, identifies abnormal behaviour, and explains the supporting signal patterns to an operator.**

Start with **one robot and one task**, such as pick-and-place. Add detailed troubleshooting only when the annotations support it.

**The next hour should produce a concrete data decision:**

1. **Inspect FactoryBench examples on the CPU VM.** Load its episode metadata and a small selection of anomaly questions with their corresponding signals. Verify that the answers are supported by those signals.
2. **Check the training interface.** Convert a few examples through TimeNet and verify that OpenTSLM receives numerical time series plus a question and target answer.
3. **Run the model smoke test on Nebius.** Confirm checkpoint loading, inference, and a tiny training batch before preparing thousands of examples.

There are two findings we must account for:

- **FactoryBench’s public release is an undivided pool.** Its `train` label does not establish a proper split. Keep every question and window from the same underlying episode together, and reserve untouched episodes for evaluation. [Dataset documentation](https://huggingface.co/datasets/FactoryBench/FactoryBench)
- **FactoryNet and FactoryBench share upstream sources, including AURSAD and voraus-AD.** Training on one and testing on the other does **not** automatically create an independent evaluation. Also exclude explicit fault labels and outcome flags from model inputs. [FactoryNet composition](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.09081v2)

**Success for that first hour:** several verified signal–question–answer examples, a clear holdout strategy, and one successful training batch. If FactoryBench’s packaging or annotation quality blocks that, use original voraus-AD with simpler, evidence-based answer templates.

I’ve checked the papers and published dataset pages; the actual loading and training checks remain to be done.

Okay, so everybody is researching until 14:45. I think we can continue but can you please explain what the data is like, what FactoryBench as well as the other dataset is, how we continue from here to get it working?

**FactoryNet provides industrial sensor recordings. FactoryBench turns robot recordings into questions and answers that a model can learn from.** For your hackathon, FactoryBench could supply both the signals and the language targets, so you may not need to combine the two initially.

**What FactoryNet data looks like**

Imagine a robot picking up an object. Its controller repeatedly records what it commanded and what happened:

| Signal group | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Setpoint** | What the robot was instructed to do | Target joint position and speed |
| **Effort** | How hard its motors are working | Current and torque |
| **Feedback** | What the robot actually did | Measured position and speed |
| **Context** | Conditions surrounding the operation | Payload, machine type, operating mode |

Each timestamp is a row; each signal is a column. A complete operation is an **episode**, containing many consecutive rows.

FactoryNet’s paper describes roughly **23,000 episodes**, combining real laboratory recordings, existing datasets such as voraus-AD and AURSAD, and simulated operations. Tasks include pick-and-place, screwdriving, and peg insertion. The published packages need checking because their contents may cover only part of the paper’s full collection. [FactoryNet paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.09081v2), [available dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Forgis/FactoryNet)

An **illustrative** abnormal pattern would be: the controller requests movement, motor current rises, but the joint barely moves. That supports describing resistance or stalled movement; it does not necessarily identify the exact broken component.

**What FactoryBench adds**

FactoryBench pairs robot telemetry with approximately **70,000 generated question–answer items**. It includes questions about:

- **State:** What is happening? Is something abnormal?
- **Intervention:** What would change after an adjustment?
- **Counterfactuals:** What might have happened under different conditions?
- **Decisions:** What should an operator investigate?

Records contain a question, an answer, sometimes answer options, signal context, and references to the source episode. The repository also includes underlying **FactoryWave** telemetry. These are constructed benchmark targets, not necessarily technician-written reports for every episode. [FactoryBench documentation](https://huggingface.co/datasets/FactoryBench/FactoryBench)

**FactoryNet is a collection of robot measurements. FactoryBench is a collection of questions about robot measurements. Neither is itself the AI model.** Your team trains the model using suitable data from them.

Think of one robot picking up a box:

- **FactoryNet supplies the recording:** commanded movement, actual movement, motor current, torque, and metadata over time.

Your team’s idea is **a robot observability assistant: someone can inspect a robot recording, ask what happened, and get an answer supported by the sensor data.**

That fits the challenge well. It also makes the language component central to the product.

**What “observability” means here**

Imagine an engineer looking at seven torque curves after a robot behaved unexpectedly. Your assistant helps answer:

- “What changed during this recording?”
- “Which joints show the strongest changes?”
- “Was the change sudden or sustained?”
- “What does the recording support, and what can’t we determine?”

The useful output is an explanation connected to the chart. For example, **illustrative—not a finding from this dataset**:

> “Joint 3 shows a sharp torque increase, followed by a smaller change in joint 4. This is consistent with a contact event. These signals alone do not identify the object involved.”

“Observability” is your product direction; you still need to choose and evaluate specific questions.

**Your description of OpenTSLM is mostly right**

More precisely, OpenTSLM **is not limited to a fixed classification or forecasting output**. It combines numerical time series with text prompts and generates language. Its documented tasks include question answering, captioning, and classification expressed through language. So identifying a collision can remain part of your task—the contribution is answering useful questions with supporting evidence. [OpenTSLM documentation](https://github.com/OpenTSLM/OpenTSLM)

“Language as a first-class citizen” means both the **question and answer** matter during training:

**Torque signals + channel descriptions + question → OpenTSLM → answer**

A fluent explanation is not automatically a faithful explanation. You will need to check its claims against the measurements.

**What your new dataset actually contains**

I checked the Zenodo metadata and accompanying README. Your link is **Raw Torque Data from Collision Experiments on a KUKA Robot, Part I: Accidental Collisions**:

| Property | What it means |
|---|---|
| Robot | KUKA LWR4+ arm |
| Signals | Torque measurements from seven joints |
| Sampling | 1,000 measurements per second per joint |
| Units | Newton-meters |
| Collection | 206 collision sequences |
| Format | MATLAB files in compressed archives |

This is raw experimental data; the documentation does **not provide a ready-made collection of natural-language questions and explanations**. Creating that layer would be part of your project. [Dataset and README](https://zenodo.org/records/21927431)

There is also a [processed quick-start dataset](https://zenodo.org/records/6461868) with accidental collision, intentional contact, and contact-free examples. Its windows are 1.024 seconds long, with collision/contact onset fixed at 0.256 seconds. That makes it convenient for initial loading experiments, but a poor test of whether a model can discover **when** an event occurred: it could simply learn that fixed position.

Your linked Part I covers accidental collisions. To compare accidental versus intentional contact, you would also need the corresponding contact data. [Author’s repository](https://github.com/zhang-zengjie/robot-raw-collision-signals)

**How I suggest moving forward**

1. **Inspect a small raw sample first.** Load and plot all seven channels; verify timestamps, event annotations, and recording identifiers. Establish what we can truthfully ask and answer before downloading everything or training.

2. **Build the TimeNet connector and language examples.** Preserve recording identity, units, channels, and annotations. Start with questions about signal changes and comparisons. Construct reference answers from verified annotations and calculated measurements, then manually review a sample. Do not invent physical causes or technician explanations.

3. **Fine-tune a small pretrained OpenTSLM.** Train on numerical signals plus questions and reference answers. Keep entire source recordings together when separating training and test data—different windows from the same recording must not cross that boundary.

4. **Evaluate and demonstrate.** Compare against a simple system that computes signal statistics and produces templated answers. Measure factual correctness, unsupported claims, and event recognition where labels support it. Also remove or shuffle the signals to check whether the model actually uses them.

The demo could show **a recording, seven curves, a question box, and an answer with highlighted evidence**.

For your next team checkpoint, aim to have **one real recording plotted and three questions with defensible reference answers**. That will establish whether this dataset supports your observability idea before you commit the remaining hackathon time to training.

An agentic ingestion pipeline strengthens it **if it demonstrably makes unfamiliar telemetry easier to use**. The core achievement still needs to be a model that answers questions correctly from signals.

Your pitch could be:

> **An observability assistant for robot operators that turns unfamiliar telemetry into queryable data and explains recorded events with evidence.**

**I would correct three details on the Notion page**

- **OpenTSLM:** Say “generates language from time series and questions, rather than being limited to a fixed classification output.” Classification can still be part of an answer.
- **Windows and onset:** Your linked dataset contains raw recordings. Approximately one-second windows would be your preprocessing choice. The *separate processed dataset* uses 1.024-second windows with a fixed event position. Verify the raw annotations before promising accurate onset identification. [Dataset](https://zenodo.org/records/21927431), [processed version](https://zenodo.org/records/6461868)
- **URDF:** The repository provides the robot’s geometry and joint structure. It can support a robot diagram with joints highlighted by measured torque changes. **Replaying actual movement requires joint positions; torque alone does not establish the robot’s pose.** Also, the joint with the largest torque change is not necessarily where contact occurred. [URDF repository](https://github.com/jkaniuka/kuka_lwr4plus_urdf)

**What the ingestion agent should actually do**

Give it a bounded job: **take a supported dataset URL or uploaded recording and prepare a validated TimeNet import.**

| Step | Useful behavior |
|---|---|
| Inspect | Read documentation and examine file structure |
| Propose | Map channels, units, sampling rate, and recording identifiers |
| Validate | Run deterministic checks for missing values, synchronization, and inconsistent metadata |
| Import | Use the connector to produce standardized data |
| Report | Show provenance, transformations, and unresolved information |

The agent chooses tools and interprets documentation; code performs the numerical checks. Unknown units or channel mappings should remain unresolved until verified.

To demonstrate reuse, test it on a second file layout with different column names or channel ordering. That is a concrete contribution. A broad web-search agent would consume more time before proving the core product.

**How I would prioritize the work**

1. **Establish the data contract first.** Load several raw recordings, plot seven channels, and verify event annotations and source identifiers. Preserve those identifiers so windows from the same recording stay in the same train/test split.

2. **Build three answerable questions.** Start with:
   - “Describe the main torque changes in this interval.”
   - “Which joints show the strongest changes relative to the preceding interval?”
   - “Compare these two intervals and explain the differences.”

   Add “When did contact begin?” only once trustworthy annotations are confirmed. Build reference answers from measured evidence and verified labels, with manual review.

3. **Get one complete training path working.** TimeNet export → numerical signals and text questions → OpenTSLM fine-tuning → answers on unseen recordings. The language targets must include evidence; merely expanding a class label into a sentence would make a weaker contribution.

4. **Develop the demo and ingestion agent alongside that path.** Show a robot diagram, synchronized curves, a selected interval, and an answer that links to supporting channels and timestamps. Keep the robot in a clearly illustrative pose unless position measurements are available.

5. **Prove the result.** Compare against a simple numerical-analysis baseline with templated answers. Evaluate factual claims, supported event labels, and unsupported assertions. Include a shuffled-signal test to check whether answers depend on the telemetry.

**The strongest demo moment:** import an unfamiliar supported recording, show the agent’s validated mapping, ask a question, and click the answer’s evidence to highlight the relevant curves and joints.

Your immediate milestone should be **one imported recording → one grounded answer → one visible piece of evidence**. Once that works, the ingestion agent and robot visualization strengthen a functioning product.

<proposed_plan>
# Robot Observability Assistant

## 1. Goal and first release

Build an assistant that lets a robot operator ask questions about recorded telemetry and receive natural-language answers with inspectable signal evidence.

The first release will use the KUKA dataset, prepare it through TimeNet, fine-tune OpenTSLM, and demonstrate improvement over the pretrained model on held-out recordings. Classification and numerical answers will be expressed through language.

**Confirmed priorities:** deliver the three evidence-based question families first. “Action classification” means identifying the interaction type; operator-action recommendations are outside this release.

The initial questions are:

1. **Describe an interval:** identify the joints with the largest torque ranges and report their extrema.
2. **Compare against a reference:** identify the largest departures from each joint’s preceding median.
3. **Compare variability:** explain which joints became more or less variable between two specified intervals.

Each answer must identify relevant joints, intervals and measurements. Avoid unsupported claims about contact location, physical causes or required repairs.

## 2. Data preparation and TimeNet integration

Use [KUKA accidental-collision recordings](https://zenodo.org/records/21927431) as the primary dataset. Start with the six inspected recordings, then expand to the full release.

- Read `MsrExtTrq`: timestamps plus seven **signed external-torque channels**. Preserve total measured torque and joint positions separately for later use.
- Validate dimensions, finite values, increasing timestamps, sampling intervals, channel synchronization and marker bounds. Quarantine invalid recordings with explicit reasons.
- Preserve recording IDs, source archive checksums, units and original annotations. Call `JK_moments` entries **publisher event markers**, not verified physical onset times.
- Implement an idempotent TimeNet connector with separate download and conversion stages. Store one full recording per TimeNet record, seven channels, annotations and question-answer tasks.
- Verify a TimeF export/reload round trip before producing model inputs. Retain full-resolution values for evidence calculations.
- Document source attribution and the discrepancy between the dataset’s license metadata and README; do not silently choose one or redistribute raw recordings.

Split recordings **before window generation**, using seed 42 and approximately 70% training, 15% validation and 15% test. Group recordings from the same experimental run when identifiable. Keep the six already inspected recordings in development data.

Produce fixed 1,024-sample windows. Include both event-adjacent and quieter intervals, vary event position within windows, and never label an interval “contact-free” solely because it falls between markers.

Initial dataset targets:

- Up to 1,200 training questions, balanced across the three families.
- 150 validation questions.
- 300 test questions across at least 20 held-out recordings.

Reference answers come from deterministic calculations on the original values. Review a diverse training sample and all test questions before freezing the benchmark. Keep test labels out of training, prompts and preprocessing decisions.

## 3. Training and evaluation

Use the audited OpenTSLM-SP implementation and `OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-1b-tsqa-sp` checkpoint. Pin source and checkpoint revisions and record the resolved base-model revision.

The training adapter supplies:

- Numerical input shaped `[7, 1024]`.
- Seven matching joint descriptions.
- A question with explicit interval boundaries.
- A concise reference answer with supporting measurements.

Fit one fixed affine scaler per joint using training data only. Preserve its parameters and explain the transformation in channel metadata so physical units remain recoverable. Compute reference answers from unscaled values.

**First GPU validation**

- Confirm CUDA and base-model access.
- Use eight reviewed training examples and two examples from separate validation recordings.
- Run 20 optimizer steps with microbatch size 1, gradient accumulation 4, AdamW learning rate `1e-4` and gradient clipping at 1.0.
- Initially train the encoder and projector with the language backbone frozen.
- Require finite losses and gradients, changed trainable parameters, successful generation, and identical greedy outputs after checkpoint reload.

Microbatch size 1 and fixed-length inputs avoid the padding problems identified in the current implementation.

After that passes, run the first substantive training experiment for 300 optimizer steps, checking validation performance every 50 steps. Select the checkpoint using validation results. Make further training changes only against validation data.

Evaluate three systems on the same frozen test set:

1. Numerical calculations with templated answers.
2. Pretrained OpenTSLM.
3. Fine-tuned OpenTSLM.

Report joint-selection accuracy, comparison-direction accuracy, numerical error in Nm, extrema-timing error, supported-fact coverage, unsupported-claim rate and generation latency. Count malformed answers explicitly.

Include paraphrased questions and signal-shuffling controls. Report uncertainty by resampling recordings, rather than treating related windows as independent.

The numerical baseline is expected to be strong on arithmetic. Published collision-classification and TSQA scores provide context; they are not directly comparable to this custom benchmark.

## 4. Demo and parallel work

Build the first interface with **Gradio and Plotly**:

- Select a recording and inspect all seven torque curves.
- Select question intervals and ask a supported question.
- Display the model’s answer beside independently calculated evidence.
- Highlight verified channel/time references. Flag unsupported claims instead of silently correcting model outputs.
- Show pretrained versus fine-tuned answers on held-out examples.

Divide implementation into three parallel workstreams after agreeing on recording and QA interfaces:

| Workstream | Deliverable |
|---|---|
| Data and TimeNet | Connector, validation report, split manifest and QA references |
| Model and evaluation | Training adapter, baseline generations, checkpoint and scoring |
| Demo and submission | Signal viewer, answer/evidence display, dataset documentation and pitch |

Finish one complete import → prediction → evidence display path before expanding features.

Deferred features have explicit gates:

- **Event type:** add intentional-contact data and reviewed background examples before comparing collision/contact/no-contact.
- **Temporal localization:** start with measurable extrema; add physical onset evaluation only after annotation precision is established.
- **3D robot:** use verified joint positions and URDF mapping for motion replay; otherwise show an explicitly illustrative pose.
- **Agentic ingestion:** after the core works, add a bounded agent that proposes mappings, invokes deterministic validators and produces a TimeNet import report. Demonstrate it on a second supported file layout.
- **External model comparison:** add ChatTS only after the three primary evaluations are complete.

## 5. Acceptance and assumptions

The first release is complete when:

- TimeNet round-trip checks preserve signals, timing and provenance.
- No recording crosses dataset splits.
- Reviewed QA references and a frozen test manifest exist.
- A trained checkpoint reloads and produces held-out answers.
- Evaluation compares pretrained, fine-tuned and numerical-baseline results.
- The demo connects generated claims to visible evidence.
- Submission includes code, connector, training configuration, checkpoint, dataset documentation, evaluation and pitch deck.

Assume one team GPU with sufficient memory, preferably 48 GB or more, and approved Hugging Face access to the base model. GPU readiness and model access remain prerequisites to confirm; data preparation and the demo can proceed independently.

Keep the first release to recorded telemetry analysis. Live robot control, maintenance recommendations and claims of precise collision-onset detection are outside its acceptance criteria.
</proposed_plan>

Build a polished, independent frontend that works with real KUKA sample data now and connects to the team’s ingestion, retrieval and inference services later through defined adapters.

The main workflow is:

**Select a recording → inspect an event → select an interval → ask a question → follow the answer’s evidence back to the signals.**

The repository already contains a React/TypeScript/Vite scaffold, initial types, design notes and an [integration proposal](/Users/sametdegirmenci/Downloads/ysamet/docs/FRONTEND_INTEGRATION.md). Dependencies are installed. The dashboard, data fixture and service adapters are not complete yet.

## 2. Interface and interactions

Use Foxglove’s compact, data-focused character, refined with Impeccable’s guidance: charcoal surfaces, thin separators, readable typography, restrained selection color and stable channel colors. Avoid decorative metric cards, gradients and fabricated activity.

Three views share the selected dataset and recording:

### Inspect — the default workspace

```text
Dataset / recording                 Connection and model status
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Recording overview + event list   │ Joint 1 torque
                                 │ Joint 2 torque
Source and selection details     │ Joint 3 torque
─────────────────────────────────│ Joint 4 torque
Assistant conversation           │ Joint 5 torque
Evidence + observable tool calls │ Joint 6 torque
Question composer                │ Joint 7 torque
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Shared timeline / selected interval / playback controls
```

**Recording explorer**
- Show the full recording, publisher markers, selected interval and compact event list.
- Display provenance, duration, units and sampling resolution as supporting information.
- Selecting a marker centers an interval around it and updates every plot and the next question’s context.
- Identify markers as publisher annotations; do not present them as confirmed onset times.

**Signal strips**
- Seven aligned plots with a shared time axis and hover cursor.
- Each plot displays joint name, Nm units, individual scale and sample value.
- Support interval selection, zoom presets and reset to full recording.
- Use extrema-preserving display decimation. Keep raw data and calculated evidence separate from display resolution.
- Evidence links select their associated time interval and highlight the relevant channels.

**Assistant**
- Default to an assistant interface designed for an LLM that can call OpenTSLM, CNN inference, statistics and retrieval.
- Show the recording and interval attached to each question.
- Display observable tool activity, final answers and evidence separately; never expose or invent private reasoning.
- Preserve each request’s original interval even if the operator changes the charts while it runs.
- Provide stop, retry and clear failure states.

Before backend integration, offer explicitly labeled **local numerical analysis** for supported questions. Do not simulate a successful model call.

**Responsive behavior**
- At 1440 × 900, keep all seven plots and the composer visible.
- At narrower widths, use Signals and Assistant sections rather than shrinking the desktop layout.
- Support keyboard event selection, labeled controls, visible focus and reduced motion.

### Data — ingestion and retrieval visibility

- Show available datasets, recordings, source links and validation reports.
- Provide dataset-search and source-import forms, ready for the ingestion service.
- Display actual stages: inspecting, mapping, validating, importing, ready, needs input or failed.
- Show retrieved documents with source references, distinct from numerical signal evidence.
- While disconnected, show clearly labeled example states and prepared requests; never suggest an import actually ran.

### Compare — model evaluation workspace

Run the same interval through available models and compare outputs in a compact table:

- **1D CNN:** classification output.
